idiom_name: class with private plain/protected std::map partitions sealed via OpenSSL EVP AEAD (or libsodium)
implementation_notes: The C++ realization is a hand-written class: private std::map<std::string, std::string> partitions for plain and protected pairs, a serialize-then-seal path over OpenSSL's EVP AEAD (AES-256-GCM) or libsodium, and an overridden to_string()/operator<< for the masked-list route. What replaces the classic structure: the seal()/unseal() member pair plus the protected-name set replaces the source pattern's two maps and masked list, while RAII (std::vector<std::byte> for the sealed blob, a small key wrapper whose destructor calls OPENSSL_cleanse) is how plaintext and key lifetimes are bounded. C++20 toolchains can use std::span and stronger type separation, but no standard type will seal an object for you, so the class boundary is the only enforcement the language offers.
pitfalls: Convenience serializers that walk every public member (nlohmann::json's default, fmt/ranges formatting, reflection-based debug output) will transcribe protected values unless the serializer is explicit or the partitions are not reachable members.
Copies and moves duplicate plaintext: implement the rule of zero/five deliberately, clear the plaintext partition after sealing, and never let a copy constructor silently resurrect it.

std::string is not wipeable: SSO keeps short secrets inside the object, reallocations leave copies on the heap, and OPENSSL_cleanse only clears the buffer you still hold - treat erasure as best-effort and use fixed-size buffers where it matters.
Exceptions thrown while a plaintext buffer is live can carry fragments into diagnostics; catch, log without payload, and keep secrets out of exception messages.
